results.question: An email from 'IT Support' says your account will be disabled and asks you to verify your password at a link. You should:
results.explanation: Never authenticate from an email link. Verify via the official app or a number you already trust.

results.question: You find a USB drive labelled 'Payroll 2026' in the parking lot. You should:
results.explanation: Dropped media is a classic baiting vector (and modern sticks can emulate a keyboard). Hand it in untouched.

results.question: A caller claims to be the helpdesk and asks you to read out the MFA code that just arrived. You should:
results.explanation: No legitimate helpdesk needs your MFA code or password. Hang up and call back on a number you trust.

results.question: A text says a parcel is held and you must pay a $1.99 fee via a link. You should:
results.explanation: Small unexpected fees are the pretext to harvest full card data. Never act on a delivery link; check the real app.

results.question: The CEO emails you to send an urgent wire transfer and says to keep it confidential. You should:
results.explanation: Business email compromise relies on secrecy and urgency to bypass process. Verify out of band; never skip controls.

results.question: Your phone is flooded with MFA push prompts you did not request. You should:
results.explanation: MFA fatigue (push bombing) means someone has your password and is trying to get you to approve. Deny and report.

results.question: Which practice best defends against credential stuffing (reusing leaked passwords)?
results.explanation: Unique passwords stop one breach from unlocking other accounts, and MFA blunts a stolen password.

results.question: A caller says they are from your bank's fraud team and asks for the one-time code to release your card. You should:
results.explanation: Banks never ask for OTPs, CVV, or passwords. A 'code we sent' request is the account-takeover pattern.

results.question: Someone without a badge follows you through the secure door carrying boxes. You should:
results.explanation: Tailgating bypasses every technical control. Challenge politely and report; you will never be penalized for it.

results.question: A colleague emails an unexpected 'Benefits' spreadsheet with a prompt to 'Enable Content' to view it. You should:
results.explanation: Macro-enabled documents are a top malware delivery vector. Confirm the sender on another channel; don't enable content.

results.question: A login page looks identical to your company SSO and shows a padlock. What is the reliable check?
results.explanation: Look-alike pages and TLS certificates are easy to fake. Read the domain and navigate to the site yourself.

results.question: How can your own social media usage help a spear-phishing attacker?
results.explanation: Public details become the personal hooks in spear-phishing. Tighten privacy settings and share less publicly.

results.question: While browsing, a site shows a pop-up: 'Your Flash/plugin is outdated - download the update now.' You should:
results.explanation: Fake update pop-ups deliver drive-by payloads. Patch only through built-in updaters or trusted vendor channels.

results.question: An unexpected email asks you to scan a QR code to 'renew your password'. You should:
results.explanation: QR codes hide their destination from hover/preview checks. Go to the official portal by typing the address yourself.
